newsitem.title: USA: Irish leader says IRA must act quickly on truce.
newsitem.headline: Irish leader says IRA must act quickly on truce.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Wednesday that the IRA must quickly declare an "unequivocal, believable and genuine" ceasefire or risk seeing its political wing left behind by multi-party talks on Northern Ireland.
Talks aimed at establishing a new system of government for the troubled province were set to resume June 3, after having been suspended pending Britain's general election on May 1.
Both the British and Irish governments have said the Irish Republican Army must resume a ceasefire before its political wing, Sinn Fein, would be allowed to participate.
The IRA, which is fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland, broke a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996.

"The pressure is on the IRA -- if they want Sinn Fein to take part in this talks process in any serious way -- to have a ceasefire very quickly, not on the 2nd of June or on the 30th of May," Bruton told reporters.
Sinn Fein would be entitled to take full part in the multi-party talks only "on the basis that the IRA ceasefire is unequivocal, believable and genuine," he added.

Bruton, who was visiting Atlanta as part of a five-day U.S. tour, said other parties set to move forward with the talks represented 85 percent of Northern Ireland's voters, compared with Sinn Fein's 15 percent minority.
"If the 15 percent doesn't turn up, the 85 percent have an obligation and a perfect right to get on with the business," he said.
"Obviously, it would be in the interests of any party that wants to influence the outcome of the talks to be there on the 3rd of June."

Earlier on Wednesday, British Prime Minister John Major also called for an IRA ceasefire. "I believe there is a way through to get all the parties to sit down together and talk provided there is a clear-cut and verifiable ceasefire by Sinn Fein and the IRA."

Major added that the talks had made little progress to date, partly because of the IRA's resumption of violence and partly because some parties -- he did not say which -- had been reluctant to take risks for fear of alienating their supporters in the run-up to an election.

When asked about the obstacles he saw to successful talks, Bruton criticised Unionist parties in Northern Ireland for adopting an approach that harkened back to the status quo of the mid-1960s, when the province was ruled from Belfast by a pro-British Unionist majority.

"There is difficulty, I think, in that the Unionists have tended not to take risks. They've tended to want to basically revert to a status quo that existed prior to 1968 but which really cannot be recreated in modern conditions," he said.
"It is seen by some that they are trying to return to a position where basically they would call most of the shots. In fact, that approach is going to have to stop."
